title: Exploring Vancouver
text:
One of the best parts of starting at UBC has been discovering Vancouver beyond the classroom. The city has a way of shifting quickly: quiet streets, mountain views, seawall walks, and busy neighbourhoods all seem to sit close together.
I’m slowly building a personal map of the places that make the city feel distinct. A walk through a new neighbourhood can turn into an afternoon of people-watching, good food, and noticing details I would have missed if I had stayed on my usual route.
There is still a lot left to explore, but that feels like part of the fun. For now, I’m learning the city one walk at a time.



A view from Vancouver.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Starting the UBC Master of Data Science program has felt like stepping into motion. There is a new rhythm to learn: new people, new tools, and a lot of questions arriving faster than answers.
The first weeks have been a mix of orientation, first classes, and the quieter work of finding a routine. What surprised me most is how quickly a broad field becomes personal once you start asking which problems you want to spend time with.
I’m still at the beginning, but I’m trying to pay attention to the process as much as the output. This journal is a place to keep those observations close.



Orientation day on campus.

title: A small look at fuel efficiency
text:
The mtcars dataset records fuel consumption and vehicle characteristics for 32 cars. I use it to ask a focused question: how does transmission relate to fuel efficiency, and what other variables might help explain the pattern?
The data is included with base R, and is originally from the 1974 US Magazine Motor Trend. No external data file is needed to render this post.

data(mtcars)
cars <- transform(
    mtcars,
    transmission = factor(am, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Automatic", "Manual"))
)
head(cars[, c("mpg", "cyl", "wt", "transmission")])

                   mpg cyl    wt transmission
Mazda RX4         21.0   6 2.620       Manual
Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6 2.875       Manual
Datsun 710        22.8   4 2.320       Manual
Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6 3.215    Automatic
Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8 3.440    Automatic
Valiant           18.1   6 3.460    Automatic


There are 13 automatic and 19 manual cars in this small sample. I compared their average miles per gallon.

group_means <- aggregate(mpg ~ transmission, data = cars, FUN = mean)
group_means$mpg <- round(group_means$mpg, 1)
group_means

  transmission  mpg
1    Automatic 17.1
2       Manual 24.4


Manual cars average higher fuel economy in this dataset. That comparison is descriptive, not causal: the transmission groups also differ in weight and number of cylinders.

boxplot(
    mpg ~ transmission,
    data = cars,
    col = c("#d7e3e8", "#e39b6b"),
    xlab = "Transmission",
    ylab = "Miles per gallon",
    main = "Fuel economy differs by transmission"
)







Figure 1: Fuel economy by transmission type in the mtcars dataset.





The plot shows that the manual group is shifted upward, although there is variation within both groups. A final check of weight helps explain why a simple transmission comparison should be interpreted carefully.

cor(cars$mpg, cars$wt)

[1] -0.8676594


The correlation between fuel economy and vehicle weight is strongly negative in this sample: heavier cars tend to use more fuel. A clear group difference is a starting point for analysis, not the end of the story.

title: What predicts iris species?
text:
The Iris dataset contains measurements for 150 flowers from three species. I use it here as a small example of how exploratory summaries can reveal which measurements separate groups.
The data comes bundled with scikit-learn, and the original dataset is attributed to the UCI Machine Learning Repository. No data file is downloaded while this post renders.

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
flowers = iris.frame.rename(columns={
    "sepal length (cm)": "sepal_length",
    "sepal width (cm)": "sepal_width",
    "petal length (cm)": "petal_length",
    "petal width (cm)": "petal_width",
})
flowers["species"] = flowers["target"].map(dict(enumerate(iris.target_names)))

Each species has 50 observations. I compared the average petal length across the three groups.

summary = (
    flowers.groupby("species")
    .agg(
        observations=("species", "size"),
        mean_petal_length=("petal_length", "mean"),
    )
    .round(2)
)

The average petal lengths differ substantially: setosa has the smallest petals, while virginica has the largest. I also checked the observed range for each species.

petal_ranges = flowers.groupby("species")["petal_length"].agg(["min", "max"]).round(2)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
flowers.boxplot(column="petal_length", by="species", ax=ax, grid=False)
ax.set_title("")
ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Petal length (cm)")
fig.suptitle("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Petal length by iris species.





The figure makes the separation visible. Setosa is distinct, while versicolor and virginica have higher but more overlapping petal lengths. This is a useful example of why a distribution plot gives more information than one average alone.

title: About Me
text:
A work in progress, intentionally
I’m Ankit, a student in the UBC Master of Data Science program. I’m using this space to make sense of the work, questions, and experiences that shape my path through data.

title: About Me
text:
Right now
I’m focused on building a strong foundation across the data science toolkit while staying close to the human questions underneath the technical ones. The most interesting problems rarely arrive in tidy columns.

title: About Me
text:
What I’m looking for
Good questions, generous collaborators, and projects where analysis can become something genuinely useful. I’m especially drawn to work that rewards both curiosity and care.

title: About Me
text:
Beyond the coursework
This site is also a practice in reflection: making room for the parts of learning that do not fit neatly into a résumé. Expect notes, experiments, and honest observations as the year unfolds.
